new_statements.quote: Los cuiba-wámonae prefieren no escribir el acento, ya que la posición del acento principal varía. Este generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra, pero las reglas no son tan sencillas. Para facilitar la lectura de esta gramática de parte de los hispanohablantes, se ha escrito el acento según las reglas de acentuación para el español. Hay solamente unas pocas pares de palabras en las que el acento distingue la una de la otra. Ejemplos: narúntaba ‘quedar’ (‘no ir con otro’) y naruntaba ‘se paró’; taxotsi ‘lo botó para él’ y táxotsi ‘estaba quemado (por el fuego)’. El contexto usualmente las distingue.
new_statements.translation: The Cuiba-Wámonae prefer not to write the accent, since the position of the main accent varies. It generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but the rules are not so simple. To make this grammar easier for Spanish speakers to read, accent has been written according to the accentuation rules for Spanish. There are only a few pairs of words in which accent distinguishes one from the other. Examples: narúntaba 'to stay' ('not go with another') vs naruntaba 'he/she stood up'; taxotsi 'he threw it away for him' vs táxotsi 'it was burnt (by fire)'. Context usually distinguishes them.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word accent falls by default on the penultimate syllable; the author warns the rules are not simple and a few lexical minimal pairs exist (accent is marginally contrastive). The 2018 dictionary by the same author restates it as 'the accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable; otherwise it is marked', adds that long polymorphemic words have one primary and several secondary accents, and that accent tends to be attracted to diphthong/triphthong syllables, usually the one nearest the end of the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kerr & Berg 2018, p. 12: 'La palabra larga tiene un solo acento primario y puede tener varios acentos secundarios'; secondary accents are visible on the component morphemes listed under V. (véase) in each entry. Kerr 1995 p. 22 says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: A few minimal pairs (narúntaba/naruntaba, taxotsi/táxotsi; dictionary adds kekoba 'be tight' / kékoba 'rub'); some words vary (wámonae/wamonae); accent attracted to diphthong/triphthong syllables; within a diphthong the first vowel is accented except ua, ue, ui (second), in triphthongs the second except aei, aeu (first) (1995 p. 24; 2018 p. 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (la palabra), including long polymorphemic words; citation/dictionary headword forms. Variety: cuiba-wámonae of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara), Casanare, Colombia (pin menepiwi sub-dialect; 1995 p. 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources (Kerr 1995; Kerr & Berg 2018) describe the Cuiba-Wámonae of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara) on the Casanare river, Colombia (pin menepiwi sub-dialect; Kerr 1995 p. 1 lists sub-dialects pin menepiwi, aitowapiwi/masiguare, wupiwi, siripuxi, mayáraxi, yarawútixi as mutually intelligible). Machal 2000 (Rosetta excerpt) and the Mosonyi works describe the Alto Capanaparo (Venezuela) dialect; Merchán 2000 the Maibén variant. All fall under cuib1242; no dialect-level glottocode assigned here.

sources.note: Introducción, 'La palabra y el acento', printed p. 12 (PDF p. 13): 'El acento generalmente cae sobre la penúltima sílaba, si no, está marcado.' Speakers usually do not mark accent, but the dictionary does because some words differ only by accent (taxotsi/táxotsi, kekoba/kékoba). Long polymorphemic words have one primary accent and may have several secondary accents; primary generally penultimate, otherwise marked (pona, wüüka, wowéi, kueikueijei, pewanojukuáein, peperǘü, pekuaratséneto); sometimes accent varies (wámonae/wamonae).
